name: Extrinsic Incentive Error
description: People often assume other people are driven mainly by pay, status, or other external rewards, while viewing their own motives as more intrinsic. The result is a self-other asymmetry in how motivation gets explained.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to gamification, employee tooling, loyalty systems, creator payouts, and policy design: teams can overbuild around money, points, or badges because they assume other people care about them more than they actually do.
prevalence_note: Common in management psychology and sometimes in behavioral-design or gamification critique, but rarely named explicitly in everyday product-design reviews.

findings.description: A 40-year meta-analysis of 183 studies (N=212,468) found intrinsic motivation is a medium-to-strong predictor of performance regardless of whether extrinsic incentives are present, and that incentives are actually LESS predictive of performance quality when directly tied to it (a 'crowding out' pattern) -- real evidence that extrinsic incentives are not as dominant a driver of performance as commonly assumed. Consistent with, but not a direct test of, Extrinsic Incentive Error's own core self-other-asymmetry claim (that people specifically over-attribute OTHERS' motivation to extrinsic incentives): this meta-analysis addresses whether incentives actually matter as much as assumed, not the lay-theory misattribution mechanism itself.
findings.source_title: Intrinsic motivation and extrinsic incentives jointly predict performance: A 40-year meta-analysis.

findings.description: Three laboratory studies and one field study found that people systematically overestimate how much others are motivated by extrinsic incentives and underestimate intrinsic motives, a self-other asymmetry that can lead principals or managers to design distorted incentive schemes.
findings.source_title: On the Social Psychology of Agency Relationships: Lay Theories of Motivation Overemphasize Extrinsic Incentives
findings.source_venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
